name: PGM3 deficiency
aliases: congenital disorder of glycosylation type PGM3

clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive glycosylation defect that produces a combined immunodeficiency overlapping clinically with the hyper-IgE syndromes
The characteristic triad is severe atopic disease (eczema, food and environmental allergy, asthma), marked blood eosinophilia, and a strikingly elevated serum IgE
Recurrent bacterial and viral infections of the skin and respiratory tract reflect the underlying immunodeficiency
Neurological involvement is a distinguishing feature, including developmental delay, cognitive impairment, and sometimes motor or sensorineural problems
Skeletal and connective-tissue abnormalities, such as short stature and dysmorphic features, may accompany the immune and neurological findings
As a congenital disorder of glycosylation it can be supported by abnormal glycosylation studies, with confirmation by genetic testing of PGM3

Care is largely supportive with antimicrobial prophylaxis, immunoglobulin replacement where antibody function is impaired, allergy and eczema management, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation considered in severe cases
reference.pathophysiology: PGM3 encodes phosphoglucomutase 3, an enzyme in the pathway that generates the sugar-nucleotide donor uridine diphosphate N-acetylglucosamine, which is essential for adding N-acetylglucosamine residues during protein glycosylation. Because glycosylation shapes the folding, stability, and function of countless glycoproteins on immune, neural, and connective-tissue cells, a hypomorphic defect in this enzyme perturbs many systems at once. In the immune compartment, altered glycosylation of receptors and signalling molecules skews lymphocyte development and function toward a type-2, allergic phenotype with high IgE and eosinophilia while impairing effective antimicrobial responses, and the same glycosylation failure disturbs neurodevelopment and skeletal growth, giving the combined immunological, neurological, and connective-tissue picture.
additionalDifferentials: STAT3 loss-of-function autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome
DOCK8 deficiency autosomal recessive hyper-IgE syndrome
Severe atopic dermatitis with reactive IgE elevation
Omenn syndrome and other combined immunodeficiencies with eosinophilia
additionalInvestigations: Serum IgE level and full blood count with eosinophil quantification
Quantitative immunoglobulins and specific antibody responses
Lymphocyte subset analysis and T-cell proliferation studies
Glycosylation analysis such as transferrin isoform studies where available
Skeletal survey or targeted imaging for connective-tissue and bony features
redFlags: Severe eczema with recurrent skin and respiratory infection and very high IgE
Progressive neurodevelopmental regression or worsening cognitive impairment
Serious or opportunistic infection indicating combined immune failure
Failure to thrive with skeletal abnormalities
reference.prognosis: The prognosis depends on the severity of the hypomorphic defect; milder cases may be managed supportively for years, whereas severe disease carries a substantial burden of infection and neurological impairment and may prompt haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, which can correct the immunodeficiency but not established neurological damage.
pitfalls: Diagnosing ordinary severe atopic dermatitis and missing the underlying immunodeficiency and neurological features
Attributing the picture solely to a hyper-IgE syndrome without considering a glycosylation disorder
Overlooking the neurodevelopmental component when the allergic phenotype dominates
Failing to assess and support specific antibody function
Assuming transplantation will reverse neurological or skeletal abnormalities
references: Stiehm's Immunologic Disorders in Infants and Children
IUIS Expert Committee classification of inborn errors of immunity
